title: Docker & DevOps
description: Running containers in production: resources, release strategies, GitOps, Terraform and secrets.
resumo: Requests are reserved, limits are ceilings: memory over the limit is OOMKilled, CPU over it is throttled.
The HPA needs CPU requests — without them it shows `<unknown>` and never scales.
Rolling update by default; blue/green for instant rollback; canary to validate with real traffic. Schema changes must work with both versions.
GitOps: the cluster follows Git; fix incidents in Git, or `selfHeal` reverts you.
Terraform state in a remote, locked, encrypted backend — never in Git.
Secrets from a vault via External Secrets; pods read env vars at startup — restart after rotation.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation: Deployments, Services, ConfigMaps and Secrets are taught in **Kubernetes & kubectl** (Essentials), and readiness, liveness and startup probes in **Kubernetes & kubectl → Intermediate** (Probes and Graceful Shutdown).

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** one pod uses all the memory of its node and the neighbors are evicted; at peak there are not enough replicas, and at night far too many.

**Concept:** requests are what the scheduler reserves for the pod (guaranteed); limits are the ceiling. Exceeding the memory limit kills the container (`OOMKilled`); exceeding the CPU limit causes throttling (slowness). For Java, align the heap with the limit using `MaxRAMPercentage`. The HorizontalPodAutoscaler adds or removes replicas based on CPU or custom metrics, which requires stateless applications.

**How it works:** set memory requests and limits; for CPU, set a request and think twice about a limit, because throttling shows up as unexplained latency.
examples.code:
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi" }
  limits:   { memory: "768Mi" }
---
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: api-orders
spec:
  scaleTargetRef: { apiVersion: apps/v1, kind: Deployment, name: api-orders }
  minReplicas: 3
  maxReplicas: 10
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target: { type: Utilization, averageUtilization: 70 }
examples.interview_question: What is the difference between requests and limits in Kubernetes?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: An HPA on CPU without CPU requests. Utilization is a percentage of the request, so with no request the HPA cannot compute it and never scales.
examples.code:
kubectl get hpa
# NAME         TARGETS         MINPODS   MAXPODS   REPLICAS
# api-orders   <unknown>/70%   3         10        3

kubectl describe hpa api-orders
# failed to get cpu utilization: missing request for cpu

# RIGHT
resources:
  requests: { cpu: "250m" }

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** every deploy is all-or-nothing: if the new version has a bug, every user hits it at once.

**Concept:** a rolling update (the Deployment default) replaces pods gradually without duplicating infrastructure. Blue/green keeps two complete versions and switches all traffic at once — instant rollback, but double the cost during the switch. A canary sends a small share of traffic (say 5%) to the new version and increases it as error and latency metrics stay healthy — the choice when you want to validate with real users and limit the impact of a bug.

**How it works:** with `maxUnavailable: 0`, a rolling update never reduces capacity; Argo Rollouts and Flagger automate canaries on Kubernetes.
examples.code:
# Controlled rolling update
strategy:
  type: RollingUpdate
  rollingUpdate:
    maxUnavailable: 0   # never below the desired capacity
    maxSurge: 1         # one new pod at a time

# Canary with Argo Rollouts (summary)
steps:
  - setWeight: 5
  - pause: { duration: 10m }
  - setWeight: 50
  - pause: { duration: 10m }
examples.interview_question: When would you choose a canary over blue/green?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Blue/green or canary with a database change that the old version cannot handle. During the switch both versions run against the same database, and rolling back to blue breaks it. Make schema changes backward compatible first (expand/contract).
examples.code:
WRONG: green drops the column "email" that blue still reads
       -> switch to green OK... rollback to blue -> errors everywhere

RIGHT: deploy 1 adds the new column (both versions work)
       deploy 2 switches the code
       deploy 3 removes the old column

subsections.subtitle: GitOps with Argo CD
subsections.description: Git as the source of truth for the cluster.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** the pipeline runs `kubectl apply` with cluster-admin credentials, nobody knows what is really running, and manual changes pile up.

**Concept:** in GitOps, the desired state of the cluster is versioned in a repository, and an agent inside the cluster (Argo CD or Flux) continuously compares Git with the cluster and syncs the differences. CI only updates the image tag in the configuration repository. You get an audit trail (each deploy is a commit), rollback with `git revert`, and fewer cluster credentials exposed to CI.

**How it works:** `selfHeal` reverts manual changes in the cluster; `prune` deletes resources removed from Git.
examples.code:
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: api-orders
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/shop/infra-config.git
    path: apps/api-orders/overlays/production
    targetRevision: main
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: orders
  syncPolicy:
    automated: { prune: true, selfHeal: true }
examples.interview_question: What is GitOps, and what is its advantage over applying manifests from the pipeline?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Fixing production with `kubectl edit` while `selfHeal` is on. Argo CD reverts the change within minutes, and the incident comes back. Change it in Git — even during an incident.
examples.code:
# WRONG during an incident
kubectl scale deploy/api-orders --replicas=10
# a few minutes later Argo CD syncs back to 3 replicas

# RIGHT: commit the change to the config repository (or pause auto-sync explicitly)

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** two engineers run `terraform apply` at the same time, and the state file ends up corrupted.

**Concept:** the state maps the code to the real resources. It must live in a remote backend (S3, GCS) with locking to prevent simultaneous applies, and it can contain secrets, so access must be restricted and encrypted. `terraform plan` shows what will change before `apply`, so infrastructure changes can be reviewed in pull requests. Modules avoid copy-paste between environments.

**How it works:** run `plan` in CI on every pull request and `apply` only after approval.
examples.interview_question: Why does the Terraform state need special care?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Committing the state file to Git. It may hold database passwords and keys in plain text, and two people applying from their own copies overwrite each other's changes.
examples.code:
# WRONG
git add terraform.tfstate

# RIGHT: a remote backend with locking and encryption; ignore local state
# .gitignore
*.tfstate
*.tfstate.*
.terraform/

subsections.subtitle: Secrets Management
subsections.description: Credentials outside the code and the images.

examples.title: Explanation
examples.explanation:
**Problem:** database passwords are in Kubernetes Secrets created by hand, nobody knows when they were last rotated, and anyone who can read the namespace can read them.

**Concept:** Kubernetes Secrets are only Base64-encoded and, by default, stored unencrypted in etcd; they must not be versioned in plain text either. In production, use a vault (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) integrated with the cluster through the External Secrets Operator, enable encryption at rest, restrict access with RBAC and rotate credentials regularly.

**How it works:** the operator copies values from the vault into a regular Secret and refreshes it on a schedule; the application keeps reading environment variables.
examples.code:
apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ExternalSecret
metadata:
  name: api-secrets
spec:
  refreshInterval: 1h
  secretStoreRef: { name: aws-secrets-manager, kind: ClusterSecretStore }
  target: { name: api-secrets }
  data:
    - secretKey: SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD
      remoteRef: { key: production/api, property: db_password }
examples.interview_question: Why are Kubernetes Secrets alone not enough?

examples.title: Common mistake
examples.explanation: Rotating the password in the vault and expecting the pods to pick it up. Environment variables are read at startup, so the pods keep the old password until they restart — and fail when the old one is revoked. Restart after the refresh (or mount the secret as a file the application rereads).
examples.code:
# The vault now has the new password; the Secret was refreshed...
kubectl exec api-orders-7d9f8 -- env | grep DATASOURCE_PASSWORD   # still the old value

# RIGHT: roll the pods after the Secret changes
kubectl rollout restart deploy/api-orders
